game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: I think Orwell as a game is a great concept, but could have been executed far better. The game highlights important information, and railroads you into making choices that aren't backed by evidence. It doesn't provide enough detail for you to make judgement calls, but leaves you between two equally plausible answers, and forces you to make a choice. A better way of doing this would have been to present more information than necessary, and let players sort out what's important, and take their own notes. I would have preferred the game to involve less bias - letting players make their own choices, and come to their own conclusion on the benefits - or invasions - of government surveillance. I also feel the ending was robbed from me. I simply couldn't figure out how to support the cause of Thought, and wanted to have to face the ethical dilemma of doing so. Instead, I had to give them in as the only way to move forward. I really wanted to like this game, but I ultimately can't recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought this game because of all the good reviews, and while the game was enticing at certain times, and it had a great premise; it's literally only 5 hours worth of gameplay and that's it. There isn't even a repetive mode like in Papers, Please where you can at least mess around in the game outside of the story. There's no sub-quests, or sub-stories. There's nothing but the very short main story and CREDITS "THANKS FOR PLAYING". The ending is very unrewarding as well.

If this game were a few bucks, I wouldn't have complained; but $10+ depending on when you bought it? I guess it's better than going to the movies (in some ways), but I was left very unfulfilled by this. If all 5 of those hours were gripping and suspenseful like the few moments in this game that were? It'd have been worth it, but it doesn't quite succeed at that.

TL;DR: Not a bad game, but only one storyline, no sub-plots, no game to be done outside of the main story. Main story is also waaaay too fast. Also not much diversity in storyline no matter what you choose/do. You are pretty much just walked through the entire storyline the whole game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I played "Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You" through in about 4 hours. Surely, it was somewhat entertaining, but I do think I should've gotten more out of it for the money. Having said that, I don't think it's impossible that I would ever replay it, considering the story can change depending on your actions. 

What I found interesting about the game was that I kept feeling that I was the main enemy - and yet I found myself enjoying the power I held. Psychologically, it was a different experience. I am happy with the ending I got. 

The main issue I had with the game was how limited I felt throughout it. Basically - you play as an investigator and loads up information to a network made to, well, spy on people. However, what information you can load up is already pre-decided by the game, which at times left the player with knowledge that couldn't be used in game. In addition, you couldn't take any data back or update it - unless the game wanted you to. The Orwell-system in the game didn't feel fully developed.

In conclusion, I feel as if the game was released before it was fully finished. I often felt frustrated, wondering why I wasn't able to upload information I found interesting, and that it felt unrealistic that such a complex system wouldn't be able to handle conflicting data. But I did find the concept interesting.

review_text_raw:
Disappointing.  

1. Incredibly short.  I was surprised when it was over, as it felt like I just completed a tutorial.
2. Hand holding the entire way through.  Your "adviser" or "controller" does just that, controls you.  All you do is drag and drop things.  You make very few decisions and are spoon fed what you need to do next.

This kills immersion and makes you, not an investigator, but just a peon dragging and dropping lines of text.
4. Game locked up for me on conclusion.  I have only played through one ending and have no desire to do the others, because the gameplay is like a tutorial from start to finish.  It would be tedious as hell playing through it again.
5. Writing is corny.  It feels like it is forcing the dialogue to be edgy and using memes.  Seriously feels like an awful episode of BBT.

So much potential, but fails the entire way through.  Definitely not worth 10 pounds.  Not even worth 5.  Maybe 1.99.  The game is incredibly short.  Steam says I played it for 7.1 hours, but the reality is I fell asleep while playing about halfway through and dozed off for a couple hours.  Even at 7 hours, the gameplay is disappointingly short.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The short review: I enjoyed playing this game, but I wouldn't recommend it. You should give it a try and form your own opinion though!

The long review: The game frustrated me because I expected a lot more narrative-wise since they used the name "Orwell". It definitely had parts where it excelled. The art is fantastic. The evidence gathering mechanic is a fun take on the traditional point and click genre. The story maintains a sense of mystery and suspense that can hook you in for the most part. Trying to figure out who Goldfels is and whether or not their intentions are truly malicious was what drove me to keep playing. I loved that there were also little easter eggs, such as a reference to "giraffes in hats" and articles about a 50 shades ripoff movie that made the game world feel more alive.

However, the writing... that's where this game falls short. There are other reviews talking about how the dialogue could be better etc., and I agree with them, but it wasn't the worst thing ever and it didn't ruin my experience. What DID ruin things for me was the game's last chapter. The narrative took a nosedive and the payoff completely ruined the setup. Most other reviews had no issue with the ending though, so you should definitely reserve your judgement and play the game first!


*****Some spoilers ahead*****

Just for context, I've only played this game once, and in my playthrough I prevented the 3rd bomb from exploding and decided to turn in evidence against Catherine Delacroix at the end.

The thing I hated MOST about this last chapter was the twist. Basically, one of the characters go "I was the person behind all those bombings bwahahaha". A real Reiner Braun moment.

This twist ending had two effects. First, it completely undermined the established mystery. Immediately, I felt stupid for caring about the game at all. What was the point of me working so hard then? Why did I collect all that evidence, if the criminal was just going to out themselves like that? 

The second effect was it made the whole narrative thematically unsatisfying. In the ending I received (I don't know if there are other possibilities), the criminal become the leader of the activist group with no repercussions. This was a person who'd set up two bombs that killed people. What pissed me off the most was that this person's friends acknowledges that this person committed murder, but based on the ending, it suggests all of them had decided to look the other way. Apparently, murder and thought manipulation is not a big deal when THEY are the ones doing it. So am I supposed to sympathise with this irresponsible group of people who have showed no regard for human life?? It's feels extremely hypocritical.

It really frustrated me because this game keeps telling me these people are innocent and I'm ruining their lives, but these people clearly aren't innocent. The worst things they did included: killing a police officer, doxxing a government agent, bombing and killing people at two separate locations, then attempting to cover up their crimes. Granted, some of these characters are more justified in their actions, but that doesn't change the fact that they actively ruined or tried to ruin people's lives. The only person I can say is mostly harmless in all of this is Themba. The game could've easily made this more nuanced by adding just one completely innocent character for the player to falsely incriminate. This one change would've easily revealed the flaws of the Orwell surveillance system, but that's not what happened. Instead, the game tries to guilt-trip you into feeling bad for outing people who have ACTUALLY done terrible things.

Maybe I only had a bad experience because my choices sucked. Maybe there is an ending where I get a better experience and justice is served to all, but then that implies there is a "right" way to choose, therefore you SHOULDN'T have the freedom to choose, your thoughts should be RESTRICTED so you choose only what the game thinks is right.

So what exactly is this game trying to tell me?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't feel like I can truly call this a detective game, or even a puzzle game. The choices available are limited (2-3 outcomes), and [spoiler] almost none of the choices that are made throughout the game affect the ending, or really the flow of the story in general[/spoiler]. Choices do not matter. [spoiler] Speaking of the ending, I felt that they were quite sudden, especially "Thoughts are free", and didn't follow entirely plausibly from the actions you took to get there. How exactly does the investigator incriminating oneself IMMEDIATELY result in the termination of Orwell? How does an incredibly sophisticated surveillance program like Orwell, even still in test phase, get torn down in a day? Never mind that there were probably backup investigators lined up, or that The Party likely would not have wanted to let go of the project so easily. If the main message of the story is that "surveillance cannot be impartial and bias will always be present", then it seems careless to throw away the secondary message - "surveillance is pervasive and nigh impossible to detect and curtail once it reaches a tipping point" - in the final moment. And yet curtail in an instant, they did. [/spoiler]

Credit where it is due, the character dialogue and writings felt very genuine, and portrayed each person convincingly.

Other reviewers have already said all of this, better. Like [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/MangoMaraudr/recommended/491950/]this one[/url].

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Okay... I don't usually write game reviews. I generally have a pretty good idea of what I'm buying beforehand on Steam, and if a game is shit it's usually because I paid for shit. But this fucking game got me.

The biggest trick is that little "Choice Matters" tag that people gave it. I love choice games. The replay value of finding every unique ending alone usually makes it worth the price. There's also something thrilling, something special to video games, when you're able to make a choice and know it matters.

Choice doesn't matter in this game.

You do ultimately get to choose what's "shown" to your supervisor, and sometimes those choices do affect the game in some way. But you're railroaded HARD through just about every major event, forced to fight for even the smallest change in dialogue from game to game. The only half-consequential "choice" you get comes at the end, and to get there you need to sit through 2+ hours of the exact same gameplay. You might as well be buying the game to play once. If you're ok with playing once and then quitting (the game does have some beautiful artwork and some really gripping moments) then by all means do so. But if you want your choices to really matter, don't buy Orwell.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- The game brings awareness to important social problems: surveillance and totalitarianism
- Music is OK
- The characters are relatable
- Story is realistic
- This implementation of mass surveillance is plausible


Cons:
- Lack of depth in decision. The game is basically linear, except the ending which is a binary moral choice. No replay value.
- Lack of immersion stemming from weak game mechanics.
- The conflict system makes no sense and works against realisticity. How in the world can the system predict that something is in conflict with an unknown data chunk? A conflict should only be shown when both data chunks are known. 
- Phone calls wait for you to tap, such as everything in this game. No time pressure or feeling of urgency.
- The web is way too small, and computer hacking is way too minimalistic to be plausible.
- The enjoyment as you progress is almost a total downward slope. I think the last episode and the ending is just not ready.
- Game lasts no more than 8 hours.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought this game with the surveillance pack while it was on sale, and boy do I regret it. This game has a fun idea, but that's about it.

First, the gameplay is very disappointing and tiring. You don't have to look for anything, as everything is highlighted. There are few choices, and you only need to click and drag on the side. Every time you put a clue into the "database," you get interrupted by a guy either mocking you for adding an "useless" piece of information or explaining what you just added and how it helps in the story line. You can never be wrong putting a clue because you get corrected or the guy confirms that the clue is correct and explains it, it just feels like you're on a tutorial mode the entire game. Also, the fact that you can't change the clues you added or erase them is a pain. You can prevent that by hovering over a clue to see what it will add, but I didn't know that because this game bugged so much that the information didn't appear until mid-game.

The story is simple and I found it okay. It has some plot twists, etc., but it is very long for its worth. There are multiple endings, and just to get one is very confusing because it feels like every possible ending is being thrown at you and you have to pick one. I already forced myself to finish one, and I don't think I will launch this game again.

Overall, if you're looking for a small investigation game or want to feel like a detective, pass on this game. It would have been a great mobile game, but is tedious on PC.

To show you how bad I felt playing this, this is my first review I have ever made. It's not that I didn't like the game; I really [u][i]disliked[/i][/u] it and forced my way until the end.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Orwell fails on a lot of levels. A lot of very fundamental writing levels. First and foremost it gives you a set of tools that allow you to see what people do on the internet and tasks you with finding the perpetrator of a bombing. You're given one prime suspect and as you progress your web of people of interest grows and grows. The principle gameplay mechanic involves choosing which specific pieces of information you choose to report to your orwellian system. Which will change how the game plays out. The first failure comes that it is often very obvious what information is going to affect what, as it is all highlighted in blue, or yellow if it conflicts with another piece of information. This is another problem. The conflict system makes very little sense most of the time. One of the first examples of the system in use involves a personal blog ran by a Person of Interest and an editorial they wrote for a newspaper. They both detail the same concept but with completely differeing opinions on the matter, and these pieces of information are considered a conflict and therefore cannot both be reported. While this specific instance makes very little gameplay difference either way it still makes no sense. Being able to report both pieces of information would have shown (at least to me) his willingness to play whatever side of an issue would get him paid, and could've sowed him as a much stronger suspect later on. Instead you have instances where you handler is confused by information you weren't able to provide them due to it being a conflict, when both pieces of information were true. This creates a very frustrating experience in trying to influence the story and with trying to keep information that is relevant to the story seperate from information that isnt. Another fundamental failing of the story telling is its ending, which if I'm perfectly honest; is godawful. To my knowledge, your choices throughout the game have no impact on the ending. There's just three buttons at the end. Push one for your ending. None of them making  a bit of sense. Right before your ending the perpetrator of the bombings reveals themselves, showing that the previous three chapters had all just been misdirection to make sure no player could possibly guess the real one and they basically say to you the player "And this is why your system doesn't work! You couldn't even figure out I was the perpetrator" When it was the game mechanics and information that was provided to you by the game that made it impossible to determine the perpetrator. They then ask you to take down the system, since you can now see it doesnt work. your other two options are to get a politician associated with your orwell system arrested, or to claim the group the perpetrator belongs to are all terrorists using out of context IMs. If you're thinking that this seems to be lacking a very obvious fourth option then I agree. My first instinct was simply to use the perpetrator admitting to instigating the bombings to get her arrested. As that would make sense, she admitted it to our face and yet there's no option present. Just the three arbitrary ones presented. In the end it was three chapters of intriguing build up for one chapter of letdowns and unguessable twists that completely kill the narrative, suspension of disbelief, and immersion. 4/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Crime investigation visual novel. It has a few game mechanics, but it mostly an interactive story. The use of the terms "episodes" in its "seasons" are accurate; you are watching, not so much playing. It is interesting, and your decisions have some effect on the story, but you are mostly following a story on rails and playing with the details. The details matter for the fate of the NPCs, but there is really just the one decision point at the end where you pick which ending you want.

If you get it in a bundle or the recent giveaway, it is not a bad time. The story has no padding, just some red herrings that you might expect in an investigative story. The use of the medium is pretty good in parts, forcing you to play the part of the ambiguous villain manipulating information and violating privacy.

I don't recommend visual novels because I do not enjoy the medium. If you would enjoy one where you get a story about government surveillance, this would be a good one for you.

Longer review at http://www.killtenrats.com/2018/09/09/orwell/

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I must say I had high expectations for this game considering the current climate of data-collection and mass surveillance. Little did I know I was in for a boring ride! 

At first, you're guided with what info can be considered relevant or not; if you make mistakes along the way your "supervior" reminds you of the mission at hand. So that's definitely a good start, especially for chapter 1. 
But then, I expected players would be gradually given more leeway as to what info to select and upload on Orwell servers. And so as the story unfolded the whole thing felt too scripted, too one-way track, and it lost its original twist. The team tries to make up for it by adding a new rule near the end; that came too late for me. 

Also, let's talk about the ending: if you're like me and you'd already figured what was really going on 2 chapters ago, it was just dragging on for too long, with all the explanations and all. Sometimes, it's best to keep it short - better, a little cryptic -, that way it leaves room for players to engage and connect the dots.
The soundtrack was nice for most of the part except when it got all ominous - a way to tell you you've come across some serious, plot-twist info: would've been nice to try and figure it out on my own.

Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game,

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
For a game of mostly dialogue, the writing is pretty bad. Dialogues are full of cliches, characters are incredibly unlikeable, especially the first character you investigate who is just a narcissistic turd. If anything, the game makes a compelling argument FOR a nanny state, because these people all suck. I also have no clue why you have a handler, as all they do is say the most inane, mindless, stupid things whenever you upload a clue. Upload a person's interest in hiking and "Oh, she likes to go outside. Interesting." It's like the most boring person in the world is looking over your shoulder watching you work and commenting. 

The gameplay is also pretty deceptive. It makes it seem like you can omit information and be subversive, but some information is required to move forward, and you don't know which until the game just stops moving forward. So if you wanted to make someone seem like they aren't a terrorist or are, you can't. Which felt like the whole point of the game? A lot of decisions, like choosing which person's photo is on their dossier, are entirely irrelevant. It's just padding to make it seem like you are doing more than you are. In fact, most of the choices you make aren't choices. The ending also gets to the exact same climax regardless.

Also a weird decision to highlight the relevant sections to upload. I was essentially just skimming every document for the highlighted bit and going 'okay, that's the part that matters' and ignoring the rest. I say this as a person that likes to read, but because it hand holds you, you just click on the tab it tells you to click (with a helpful red exclamation mark) then click the text it tells you to click, and if there ever IS a decision, like two conflicting pieces of information that might make someone seem bad, it helpfully tells you not to make a mistake and wait until you get more info to submit that info, basically cutting out the only agency you might have as a player.

Good idea, but executed poorly.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought Orwell (on sale) expecting a sort of 1984 screens, eyes, with wiretaps everywhere. What I got was a message pop up game with a pretty compelling story. In that sentence, I just described the whole review. If you didn't get it - keep reading!

They say it's wrong to assume, and definitely after playing this, it's wrong to make assumptions sometimes. If there is a demo available, try it! This one didn't have it, and it was on sale - so I went for it. The [b]story[/b] is pretty good and well thought out, and has some serious twists and turns as it progresses. The characters are interesting and the game does a good job to keep the player guessing. The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. 

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though.

Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope.  

This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.

review_text_raw:
The game's got a very interesting premise and some cool ideas, but I think the execution falls flat - especially towards the end. My main problem - you're very limited in the sort of information that you can flag for the investigation. You can only pick pieces of texts, and their meaning in the investigation's context will be pre-decided. This was very annoying at the end - I figured out the main-man, the whodunit - but I couldn't incriminate them, the game didn't consider evidence that I inferred from as evidence. [spoiler] It's infuriating to see the bomber walk free when I tried to pick the morally good ending [/spoiler]

These game-mechanics just can't reflect the depth and complexity of a would-be mass-surveillance system, and the story and your choices have to bend to these limitations. Pick this up if you're interested - it is kinda thought provoking, but don't expect a cohesive story that reflects your choices well.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
An ultimately disappointing game. It's very short (~3 hours for a full run even if you are taking your time and reading everything), which I can forgive if the game is excellent but it's not.

The gameplay itself, as others have noted, is drag-and-drop pre-highlighted bits of text. Some of this text is mandatory for the game to proceed, some of it is optional. It's not always clear which, so it's easy to get stuck if you are doing a replay and want to see what happens if you ignore bits of evidence, and you may accidentially find yourself doing the same thing that you did last time.

A lot of the choices you make (up until episode 5) are relatively inconsequential, you'll get different text but the overall plot remains the same. Unfortunately there's no way to replay an episode to see what would happen if you did something else; supposedly this feature is being worked on, but in a choice-driven game this should have been a feature that shipped; Tell Tale has had this feature since The Walking Dead season 1.

I thought this game was going to be more about the surveillance state ala 1984, Person of Interest, etc. but I wouldn't say this is a good critique. True, you are reading other people's emails, but we're not investigating some political dissidents who said bad things about Great Leader, we're investigating an actual in-universe violent incident (and someone who potentially wants to commit more of these.) So while snooping through the emails of the suspects, it's not unreasonable to think that you are trying to catch people who legitimately committed a real crime. The game does try to railroad you a bit to force you to investigate someone who may not be the offender, which you can ignore, but this is pretty late in the game.

Some of the story beats just don't work; for instance, in the final parts of episode 4, [spoiler]information about your handler is leaked and the game forces you to drag-drop some of his personal information into his file. There's zero reason to actually do this, it's only to force the user to involve someone who clearly isn't a related to the crimes. And that would work if it was optional, but it's not. It's a "you are meant to feel bad right now" bit, and just falls flat.[/spoiler]

The "good ending" is pretty trash, [spoiler]everyone sings the freedom song and topples down statues and gives you a plaque for spilling the beans, ask Snowden how that's working out for him. It's rather corny.[/spoiler]

Overall had decent potential and the demo (episode 1) is pretty good, but fails in the end stretch.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is one of those games I played several years ago, that still elicits a groan of disgust everytime I see it in my games library. 

The game concept itself sounds extremely interesting and intriguing, but the game itself doesn't care as much about the game mechanics as it does the uninteresting writing about its unlikeable cast. All of the characters I quickly grew to dislike as I felt they were caricatures of what an amateur creative writer thought 'interesting' people would act like. I dislike the geometric art style and feel it feels particularly dated (though I've never liked it), but that's more of a personal taste.

The first act was the strongest as I hadn't grown tired of the writing yet, and the plot hadn't started indulging in it's pointless conspiracy drivel that dominates the later acts. The writing wears its politics on its sleeves with the implicit assumption that the player shares the authors values which even if you do will feel grating. 

The ending and climax are the worst offenders because what should feel like a reward for finishing the game just felt unrewarding and absurd. It eschews all world-building and you have to accept the conceit that there's only like 20 people in its world. Consequences are divorced from logic and it feels terrible. Granted I know there are multiple endings, however to reach another one I would have to play through this terrible game again, and it's simply, completely not worth it. 

I recommend avoid.

There is no game here at all, none. Instead, it's about dragging blue text onto peoples records, and then your supervisor, who speaks less with the tone of a long time bureaucrat that is spying on people, and more like a wet blanket that instantly talks with you extremely casually. Worst still, it makes government surveillance severely underpowered compared to reality.

I'm just glad that i didn't buy the second game.

I really wanted to like this but it felt obtuse at times, like I was playing a really long demo. I really enjoyed the concept though. If this game's on sale and you've nothing to do i'd definitely recommend giving it a go, but otherwise i wouldn't really recommend it.
